blocks.text: That ܥܘܕܐ is the name of the little owl Michaelis (in the Supplemm. vol. IV p. 1239) also confirms from the testimony of the Antiochene Arab, who, rendering the Syriac, translates in Psalm CII هامة [hāma] as eagle owl; and also from Ephrem the Syrian, who indeed, as is well known, does not explain the name literally, but undoubtedly understands the little owl, since he adds these spiritual remarks: that it is an image of adulterers and thieves, because this bird flies by night, just as adulterers make use of the protection of darkness. T. I. p. 276. Cf. O. G. Tychsen on the Physiologus Syrus, Chapter 21, p. 115.
Nevertheless Michaelis (loc. cit. p. 1242) thinks that this very קריא is correct, as indicating a clamorous bird.

That the Talmudists rightly interpret the Chaldeans' קפופא as eagle owl or little owl is established also by the authority of the Samaritan Arabic translator, who, where the Aramaeo-Samaritan has קפופה, puts بوم [būm], as J. D. Michaelis, loc. cit., reports from a letter of Adler sent to him.

In support of this opinion, confirmed by the authority of so many ancient translators, there is also the fact that the כוס in Ps. CII, 7. is described as a bird inhabiting ruins, חרבות, the proper abode of little owls, whence among the Arabs too it is called ام الخراب [umm al-kharāb]. This is aptly observed by Michaelis, loc. cit., who should by all means be consulted on this word.
